The eastern chipmunk (Tamias striatus) is a small, diurnal sciurid whose life history has been well documented in both field and captive settings. Under the typical active body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], gestation proceeds rapidly, with a gestation time of 31 days [tg = 31 days]. This brief uterine period is characteristic of many ground-dwelling squirrels and results in the birth of altricial neonates. Newborn pups weigh approximately 3.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.4 grams], a mass that reflects the relatively short gestational investment and the subsequent heavy reliance on maternal lactation. The altricial condition of these neonates necessitates an extended period of nursing and maternal care within the subterranean burrow system.

The early developmental phase following parturition is characterized by rapid mass gain and physiological maturation. During the nursing period, mother chipmunks invest substantial resources into their litter, and this effort culminates in weaning, when the young achieve nutritional independence. The time since birth at weaning is 36 days [tx = 36 days], occurring at the typical body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. At weaning, female offspring have attained a wet weight of approximately 50.5 grams [Wwx = approximately 50.5 grams], representing a nearly fifteen-fold increase from their birth weight. This accelerated growth trajectory is critical for juveniles to prepare for their first winter, as they must accumulate sufficient fat reserves before entering hibernation.

Sexual maturation in this species shows a pronounced sex difference in timing. Under the species' typical thermoregulatory set point of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], female chipmunks reach puberty at 187 days since birth [tp = 187 days since birth], which coincides with the spring following their birth year for individuals born in mid-summer. Males, however, exhibit a delayed developmental schedule, attaining puberty at 228 days since birth [tp = 228 days since birth] at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. This sexual bimaturism is hypothesized to relate to the greater energetic demands of male-male competition for territories and access to estrous females, requiring a longer period of somatic growth before reproductive effort begins.

The reproductive output of Tamias striatus is optimized around a relatively short active season. A female chipmunk typically produces 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5 pups per litter], and in regions with a sufficiently long growing season, she may produce 1.5 litters per year [F_R_i = 1.5 litters per year]. This reproductive frequency is constrained by the necessity of both gestation and lactation to occur within the snow-free months at the species' typical thermoneutral body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. The combination of moderate litter size and multiple litters per season reflects a strategy that balances high offspring investment with the potential for rapid population turnover in a fluctuating environment.

Longevity in the eastern chipmunk is considerable for a small rodent. The maximum lifespan, recorded under the species' active metabolic temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], is 3,467 days [am = 3,467 days], a remarkably long duration that exceeds nine and a half years. This extended lifespan is associated with a relatively slow pace of life compared to many murid rodents of equivalent body size. The asymptotic mass of 96 grams [Wwi = 96 grams] places adult females among the larger-bodied members of the genus Tamias, a size that likely reflects the energetic demands of caching behavior and overwintering survival rather than reproductive output alone. This relatively large adult body mass, combined with the species' longevity and its modest reproductive output, places Tamias striatus along a slower life-history continuum within the Sciuridae family.
